headlines.title: Sea lion dies at San Francisco beach amid surge in toxic algal bloom cases
headlines.description: A California sea lion died at San Francisco’s Crissy Field on Monday after showing signs of domoic acid poisoning, according to The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. Callers first reported the large sea lion on the beach showing signs of distress, including head weaving and seizures, about 8 a.m. A trained responder from the marine mammal center was dispatched to assess the animal and manage the scene at Crissy Field, a public waterfront area east of the Golden Gate Bridge. While the center was organizing a rescue team, however, the sea lion unfortunately died on the beach, a center spokesperson said. Samples were taken to determine if the animal was suffering from domoic acid poisoning, but the results won’t be available on Monday, according to the center. The Marine Mammal Center has seen a flare-up of sea lions stranding with signs of domoic acid poisonings this year, primarily California sea lions. Domoic acid is produced during certain harmful algal bloom events. The neurotoxin accumulates in small fish, like sardines and anchovies, which are then eaten by marine mammals like sea lions in large quantities. Since Aug. 24, about 40 sea lions have been rescued in Monterey County and southern Santa Cruz County, with additional rescues in San Mateo, San Francisco, Marin and Sonoma counties. A handful of northern fur seals have also been affected. The center said it has already passed its average annual number of domoic acid rescues — normally about 75-90 animals per year across a 600-mile California response range. “As we are currently seeing intense surges of domoic acid along the California coast, our hotline is inundated with reports of animals in need to the tune of 3-6x our normal call volume, with some days seeing nearly 700 calls,” the center said in a statement. In sea lions, the brain is attacked by domoic acid, causing seizures and heart failure. When it’s untreated, it usually causes permanent brain damage, according to the marine mammal center. The toxin will naturally flush from an animal’s system over time, but sea lions repeatedly exposed to the toxin will suffer longer-lasting and more serious effects. Domoic acid also affects humans who eat contaminated crab, shellfish and fish, causing a life-threatening condition known as amnesiac shellfish poisoning, the marine mammal center said. People and their pets should keep their distance from stranded or distressed marine mammals and call the center’s hotline, if they are located between Mendocino and San Luis Obispo County, at 415-289-SEAL (7325). More information is available at https://www.marinemammalcenter.org/ .

headlines.title: ‘You Can See Everything': New film follows Elizabeth Holmes weeks before prison
headlines.description: A new documentary involving former Theranos CEO and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has left Silicon Valley buzzing and stunned. “You Can See Everything” is a documentary about the final weeks before Holmes went to prison. In fact, she invited a documentary crew into her home to follow her and her family around. People are now wondering why Holmes would invite a film crew after being found guilty of fraud and sentenced to more than a decade in prison. “I think it’s going to give us a window into the makeup of some people who fit the profile of Elizabeth Holmes, superstars from a very young age,” said Aron Solomon, chief strategy officer for Amplify. “Look at all the 30 under 30 people since Elizabeth Holmes that have been charged with crimes. I think it’s going to give us some insight into their psychological makeup, with Elizabeth Holmes as an exemplar.” A24, who produced the film, is set to release the documentary in theaters in October. Holmes went to prison in Texas in 2023. She was sentenced originally to more than 11 years, but ended up with 10 years and three months. headlines.title: Bay Area firefighters traveling to New York City for 9/11
headlines.description: Firefighters from the Bay Area are traveling to New York City to honor the lives lost on 9/11 25 years ago. The first responders also want to honor the hundreds of firefighters who have died since then from toxic dust and other illnesses contracted at Ground Zero. Janelle Wang has more, including a closer look at a Bay Area honor guard, in the video above. headlines.title: Warming trend sparks heat advisory for Bay Area and Central Coast
headlines.description: A heat advisory will be in effect for the Bay Area by midweek when rising temperatures are expected to peak. The National Weather Service said the heat advisory will start 10 am. Wednesday through 10 p.m. Thursday for the Bay Area and Central Coast. Temperatures are expected to range from 90-105 degrees in the interior, with the coast seeing mid-70s to low-90s. Get your full Microclimate Forecast at nbcbayarea.com/weather. headlines.title: 2 people stabbed following dispute in Sunnyvale
headlines.description: Police are investigating after two people were stabbed following a dispute in Sunnyvale late Sunday night. The stabbing was reported at about 11:33 p.m. in the area of 756 San Juan Drive, according to the Sunnyvale Department of Public Safety. Authorities said the two victims were involved in a dispute with a suspect that escalated into an altercation. Both victims were stabbed multiple times before taking off from the scene. The victims called 911 and were taken to a local hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The case remains under investigation, authorities said.

headlines.title: Highway 101 reopens in San Francisco after Labor Day weekend closures
headlines.description: Highway 101 through San Francisco reopened Monday morning following three days of closures for repaving work. The northbound lanes had been closed as Caltrans crews worked to restore the highway surface, forcing Labor Day weekend drivers to use alternate routes around the work zones. The project included repaving the highway and replacing rebar beneath the new asphalt. A Caltrans spokesperson said Sunday night that crews were waiting for newly poured concrete to cure and harden enough to withstand the weight of traffic. Caltrans said the work was scheduled for the holiday weekend because traffic volumes are typically lower along that stretch of highway during the long weekend. The agency is expected to provide an update Monday morning on the project and additional closures planned for more work along the same stretch of Highway 101 in two weeks.

headlines.title: Authorities investigate another possible mountain lion sighting in San Francisco
headlines.description: A mountain lion sighting near Fell and Baker Saturday night prompted a big response. On Sunday, Animal Care and Control said the threat appears to be over; however, authorities said there was an unconfirmed mountain lion sighting on Sunday. Peter Tira with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife says they were among those called in on Saturday, but never actually saw a mountain lion. They monitored the tree and checked back again Sunday morning. Tira says it does not mean there was not a lion, as one was spotted in the Pac Heights area in January, captured and released back into the wild. “They typically come from the coast, from the Peninsula where there is a good population of lions and they can move up through the Peninsula up into wild habit, the wilder natural habitat, if you look at the map, the Panhandle is kind of connected to Golden Gate Park,” Tira said. He says it’s impossible to say where it went but the panhandle is connected to a lot of habitats leading all the way to the coast. So, the best-case scenario is that it follows the same path back. On Sunday, Animal Care and Control said there’s no longer a threat and it is believed the animal left the area. Hours later, authorities said someone reported a mountain lion sighting in the area of 44th and Fulton at 3 p.m.

headlines.title: Federal workers hold Labor Day rally in San Francisco
headlines.description: Some people in San Francisco are spending Labor Day calling for better wages and decrying what they say is “rising authoritarianism” in the United States. The rally at the federal courthouse is part of a renewed push to embrace the city’s activist Labor Day traditions, which date back to the 19th century. But Monday morning’s rally is unlike the old Market Street union parades and Labor Day picnics that were holiday traditions for decades. Instead, the rally is more reminiscent of San Francisco’s earliest labor demonstrations, which date back to the late 1860s — more than two decades before Labor Day became a federal holiday. NBC Bay Area’s Thom Jensen has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Risk of rip currents, sneaker waves along coast through Monday night
headlines.description: While many people are headed towards the water during the long weekend over the Labor Day holiday, the National Weather Service is warning people to be cautious and plan ahead if they are heading out to the coast. The NWS has a beach hazards statement in effect all along the coast, as well as around San Francisco and Marin beaches, citing a risk of rip currents and sneaker waves. Forecasters say wave heights could reach 10 feet during this time. People are urged to stay out of the water and off of rocks, jetties, and piers. The hazardous beach conditions are expected to remain in place through 11 p.m. Monday night. For people who do decide to head to the beach, Anamaria Navarrete, a National Weather Service Bay Area meteorologist, advised, “always be mindful of what areas of the beach are wet, so if you see wet jetties and wet rocks, it’s probably best to stay away from those and stay clear of those areas because that’s how far the ocean can crash up against the coast.” She also noted that for anyone considering getting on a boat during this time, to research the conditions before deciding to go out on the water because some locations are under a small craft advisory. Navarrete noted that these risks for rip currents and sneaker waves are fueled by the swell from tropical cyclones far away in the Pacific Ocean. Additionally, the NWS warned the public that low-lying areas in Marin County could see some coastal flooding on Sunday evening. NBC Bay Area crews in the Marinship area of Sausalito watched the water levels rise substantially Sunday evening at high tide, and additional water pooled into streets and parking lots there near the waterfront.

headlines.title: 2 dead after SUV crashes into embankment in Solano County
headlines.description: Two people died after their vehicle left the road and crashed into an embankment in Solano County Sunday, the California Highway Patrol said. CHP said they received a 911 call just before 12:30 p.m. regarding a vehicle that had traveled off the roadway on eastbound Interstate 80 near the Highway 113 interchange. A preliminary investigation determined that a 2011 black Infiniti FX35 SUV was traveling eastbound on I-80 when it veered off the roadway and crashed into an embankment on the right shoulder, according to authorities. Authorities said the driver, who was a 56-year-old woman from Dixon, died at the scene, and the 65-year-old male passenger died while en route to the hospital. A witness to the crash reported that the driver appeared to be asleep at the wheel just before the SUV left the roadway, CHP said.

headlines.title: San Jose adds medical personnel to EDM festival after medical emergencies
headlines.description: Another major EDM festival was underway Sunday at the same San Jose venue where 14 people were hospitalized on Friday. This time, the city says additional medical personnel are on site as thousands gather at Discovery Meadow. Authorities made the decision to add medical personnel as thousands return to Discovery Meadow to see DJs like Ian Asher and Alan Walker. That response comes after Friday night’s Chainsmokers concert, when 14 people were taken to local hospitals. San Jose Fire says it was called to Discovery Meadow just after 8 p.m. Friday for multiple people needing medical attention. Firefighters called in an ambulance task force, two additional advanced life support units and a battalion chief. 14 ambulances responded. Several people were treated for suspected alcohol intoxication and drug-related issues. Sunday, the city prepared for another large crowd. The mayor’s office said that its understanding from San Jose police and fire is that additional medical personnel are on site as Sunday’s outdoor concert is expected to draw thousands from across the Bay Area. NBC Bay Area reached out to the event organizers for their specific safety and medical plans following Friday night’s response but have not heard back.

headlines.title: Fourth annual Lowrider Day returns to downtown San Jose
headlines.description: Lowriders will cruise into downtown San Jose this weekend, bringing a piece of East San Jose’s Chicano culture to City Hall for an afternoon of custom cars, music and celebration. San Jose Lowrider Day returns Sunday for its fourth year, marking the anniversary of the City Council’s decision to repeal a decades-old cruising ban. The celebration — hosted by the offices of Councilmembers Anthony Tordillos and Peter Ortiz, as well as the United Lowrider Council of San Jose — will run from noon to 6 p.m. on Santa Clara Street between Third and Seventh streets in front of City Hall. It will feature lowriders, live music, food and local vendors, community resources and performances throughout the afternoon. At a Tuesday meeting, councilmembers officially proclaimed Sunday as 2026 Lowrider Day. But for members of the United Lowrider Council of San Jose, the annual event is about more than showing off cars. Ricardo Cortez, a member of the lowrider council who handles history and youth education, said it’s an opportunity to reclaim a culture that has long been stereotyped as criminal and show how lowriding has become an important part of San Jose’s cultural identity. Negative stereotypes can cause people to make assumptions about people simply because of the cars they drive, he said. “I think it really comes down to being able to take back the negative narratives that have surrounded lowrider culture for a very long time,” Cortez told San Jose Spotlight. “I think every year it gets bigger. It gets more popular.” The lowrider council has tried to counter negative perceptions through community events and educational presentations at schools and colleges. Cortez teaches students about the origins of lowriding, historically significant cars, hydraulics and San Jose’s role in the culture. He also wrote a children’s book, “The ABCs of Lowriding,” that he uses in his presentations. “I think a lot of it has to come down to the older generation, meeting the youth where they’re at and trying to inspire them to want to continue this tradition,” Cortez said. The celebration also represents a shift in the city’s relationship with the culture of lowriders and cruising. Cruising has been part of Chicano culture since the 1940s, and grew to be a symbol of Mexican American resistance against discrimination during the civil rights movement of the 1960s and 70s. But by the 1990s it had become associated nationally with gang violence and illegal activity, leading to cities across the U.S., including San Jose, to create laws prohibiting cruising. San Jose had a cruising ban for decades before the city council repealed it in 2022, in part due to the efforts of police officer and then-Councilmember Raul Peralez, who experienced discrimination in his youth from the cruising ban. The annual Lowrider Day grew out of that change, David Polanco, president of the United Lowrider Council of San Jose, said. “(San Jose is not) the capital of lowriding, but we’re definitely a pillar of lowriding here within the lowrider world,” Polanco told San Jose Spotlight. Polanco said the lowrider council has worked to build relationships with city agencies, nonprofits, schools and other community organizations. The group also works with the San Jose Police Department when organizing events and cruises. Councilmember Ortiz, who grew up in East San Jose, said he remembers seeing lowriders in his neighborhood, particularly around King and Story roads and during Cinco de Mayo and other cultural celebrations. “We still, unfortunately, have a stigma in the greater community against lowriders,” Ortiz told San Jose Spotlight. He said many lowrider and cruising enthusiasts are working professionals with families, adding that public events can help residents see the people behind the cars rather than stereotypes. For Ortiz, bringing the celebration to City Hall and partnering with SJPD to plan events and organized cruises is part of that shift. “I’m just excited for our Chicano community to be full front here at City Hall, at the people’s house, to display the beautiful and significance of the Chicano culture here in the city of San Jose,” Ortiz said. Editor’s note: This story was originally published by San Jose Spotlight.
